claim: Axonal degeneration is a central pathological feature of multiple sclerosis.
source: Axonal degeneration is a central pathological feature of multiple sclerosis and is closely associated with irreversible clinical disability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact about MS pathology.

claim: Axonal degeneration is closely associated with irreversible clinical disability in multiple sclerosis.
source: Axonal degeneration is a central pathological feature of multiple sclerosis and is closely associated with irreversible clinical disability.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established relationship.

claim: AxCaliber is sensitive to acute axonal damage in rats.
source: AxCaliber is sensitive to acute axonal damage in rats, as demonstrated by a significant increase in the mean axonal caliber along the targeted tract, which correlated with neurofilament staining.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing significant increase in mean axonal caliber and correlation with neurofilament staining.

claim: There is a significant increase in the mean axonal caliber along the targeted tract in rats with axonal damage.
source: AxCaliber is sensitive to acute axonal damage in rats, as demonstrated by a significant increase in the mean axonal caliber along the targeted tract, which correlated with neurofilament staining.
evidence: This is demonstrated by experimental measurements in the rat model.

claim: Mean axonal caliber measured by AxCaliber correlates with neurofilament staining in rats.
source: AxCaliber is sensitive to acute axonal damage in rats, as demonstrated by a significant increase in the mean axonal caliber along the targeted tract, which correlated with neurofilament staining.
evidence: This correlation is demonstrated by comparing MRI measurements with immunohistochemistry.

claim: Increased mean axonal diameter is associated with acute axonal pathology as confirmed by electron microscopy.
source: Electron microscopy confirmed that increased mean axonal diameter is associated with acute axonal pathology.
evidence: This is confirmed by electron microscopy measurements in the rat model.

claim: There is a diffuse increase in mean axonal caliber in most areas of the normal-appearing white matter in humans with multiple sclerosis.
source: In humans with multiple sclerosis, we uncovered a diffuse increase in mean axonal caliber in most areas of the normal-appearing white matter, preferentially affecting patients with short disease duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MRI measurements in MS patients compared to controls.

claim: The increase in mean axonal caliber in normal-appearing white matter preferentially affects MS patients with short disease duration.
source: In humans with multiple sclerosis, we uncovered a diffuse increase in mean axonal caliber in most areas of the normal-appearing white matter, preferentially affecting patients with short disease duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis showing association with disease duration.

claim: MRI-based axonal diameter mapping is a sensitive and specific imaging biomarker that links noninvasive imaging contrasts with the underlying biological substrate.
source: Our results demonstrate that MRI-based axonal diameter mapping is a sensitive and specific imaging biomarker that links noninvasive imaging contrasts with the underlying biological substrate, uncovering generalized axonal damage in multiple sclerosis as an early event.
evidence: This is concluded based on the validation in rats and application in MS patients.

claim: Generalized axonal damage in multiple sclerosis is an early event.
source: Our results demonstrate that MRI-based axonal diameter mapping is a sensitive and specific imaging biomarker that links noninvasive imaging contrasts with the underlying biological substrate, uncovering generalized axonal damage in multiple sclerosis as an early event.
evidence: This is inferred from the finding that axonal damage is greater in patients with short disease duration.

claim: Axonal damage is the main pathological substrate of irreversible neurological disability in multiple sclerosis.
source: Axonal damage is the main pathological substrate of irreversible neurological disability in multiple sclerosis (MS).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: In MS, axonal damage can be direct or secondary to demyelination, glial activation, or exposure to excitatory amino acids and cytokines.
source: In MS, axonal damage can either be direct or secondary to demyelination, glial activation, or exposure to excitatory amino acids and cytokines (Haines et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The transition to progressive MS occurs when an axonal loss threshold is reached and the brain compensatory capacity is surpassed.
source: As the transition to progressive MS occurs when an axonal loss threshold is reached, and the brain compensatory capacity is surpassed (Criste et al., 2014), the development of novel in vivo, noninvasive strategies for characterizing axonal microstructure becomes essential for early disease detection.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Conventional diffusion MRI is unspecific to different tissue compartments, such as axons or myelin.
source: However, conventional diffusion MRI is unspecific to different tissue compartments, such as axons or myelin (De Santis et al., 2014), hampering the ability to distinguish axonal damage from other microstructural changes.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Conventional diffusion MRI hampers the ability to distinguish axonal damage from other microstructural changes.
source: However, conventional diffusion MRI is unspecific to different tissue compartments, such as axons or myelin (De Santis et al., 2014), hampering the ability to distinguish axonal damage from other microstructural changes.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of specificity to tissue compartments.

claim: Validation of imaging findings is rarely performed due to limitations of quantitatively comparing in vivo to ex vivo data.
source: In addition, due to the limitations of quantitatively comparing in vivo to ex vivo data, validation of imaging findings is rarely performed (Horowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Animal models recapitulating specific aspects of MS pathophysiology are available.
source: While animal models recapitulating specific aspects of MS pathophysiology are available (Torkildsen et al., 2008, Constantinescu et al., 2011), none focuses on axonal damage but rather on the demyelinating aspect of the disease.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: No available animal model of MS focuses on axonal damage but rather on the demyelinating aspect of the disease.
source: While animal models recapitulating specific aspects of MS pathophysiology are available (Torkildsen et al., 2008, Constantinescu et al., 2011), none focuses on axonal damage but rather on the demyelinating aspect of the disease.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AxCaliber is an advanced imaging framework able to estimate an MRI axonal diameter proxy.
source: AxCaliber is an advanced imaging framework able to estimate an MRI axonal diameter proxy (Assaf et al., 2008), which has become applicable in humans thanks to recent hardware advances (Jones et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: AxCaliber has become applicable in humans thanks to recent hardware advances.
source: AxCaliber is an advanced imaging framework able to estimate an MRI axonal diameter proxy (Assaf et al., 2008), which has become applicable in humans thanks to recent hardware advances (Jones et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: AxCaliber has revealed a higher axonal diameter proxy in the normal-appearing white matter of the corpus callosum of MS patients compared to healthy controls.
source: AxCaliber has revealed a higher axonal diameter proxy in the normal-appearing WM (NAWM) of the corpus callosum of MS patients compared to healthy controls, which was interpreted as a sign of axonal damage (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Higher axonal diameter proxy in the corpus callosum of MS patients was interpreted as a sign of axonal damage.
source: AxCaliber has revealed a higher axonal diameter proxy in the normal-appearing WM (NAWM) of the corpus callosum of MS patients compared to healthy controls, which was interpreted as a sign of axonal damage (Huang et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In its original formulation, AxCaliber is only applicable to voxels characterized by a single fiber orientation.
source: However, in its original formulation, AxCaliber is only applicable to voxels characterized by a single fiber orientation (such as the corpus callosum, as in Huang et al., 2016), while at least 70% of brain voxels contain two or more dominant fiber orientations (Jeurissen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: At least 70% of brain voxels contain two or more dominant fiber orientations.
source: However, in its original formulation, AxCaliber is only applicable to voxels characterized by a single fiber orientation (such as the corpus callosum, as in Huang et al., 2016), while at least 70% of brain voxels contain two or more dominant fiber orientations (Jeurissen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A modified AxCaliber model can map whole-brain MRI axonal diameter proxy.
source: Recently, we used a modified AxCaliber model to map whole-brain MRI axonal diameter proxy (De Santis et al., 2019b), hence providing a means to characterize the axonal damage in MS in a whole-brain fashion.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Measuring a higher estimated MRI axonal diameter proxy in MS does not, per se, represent conclusive evidence of axonal damage.
source: From a pathophysiological point of view, measuring a higher estimated MRI axonal diameter proxy in MS does not, per se, represent conclusive evidence of axonal damage, especially in the light of the known bias toward larger axons of MRI-based axonal diameter quantification (Horowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a limitation and supported by citation.

claim: MRI-based axonal diameter quantification has a known bias toward larger axons.
source: From a pathophysiological point of view, measuring a higher estimated MRI axonal diameter proxy in MS does not, per se, represent conclusive evidence of axonal damage, especially in the light of the known bias toward larger axons of MRI-based axonal diameter quantification (Horowitz et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: MRI sensitivity to axonal pathology is yet to be fully demonstrated to establish its clinical utility.
source: Indeed, MRI sensitivity to axonal pathology is yet to be fully demonstrated to establish its clinical utility.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: An approach to selectively manipulate specific microstructural aspects of the parenchyma through targeted, unilateral injection of neurotoxic agents has been proposed.
source: Recently, an approach to selectively manipulate specific microstructural aspects of the parenchyma through targeted, unilateral injection of neurotoxic agents has been proposed (Garcia-Hernandez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Fourteen days after injection of ibotenic acid into the hippocampus, there is a significant increase in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy in the fimbria of the injected hemisphere compared to the control (p=0.021).
source: Fourteen days after injection of the neurotoxin ibotenic acid into the hippocampus, paired t-test revealed a significant increase in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy (p=0.021) in the fimbria belonging to the injected hemisphere compared to the control (Figure 1e), confirming that the damage affected a large portion of the tract.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis of MRI data and shown in Figure 1e.

claim: The damage from ibotenic acid injection affected a large portion of the fimbria tract.
source: Fourteen days after injection of the neurotoxin ibotenic acid into the hippocampus, paired t-test revealed a significant increase in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy (p=0.021) in the fimbria belonging to the injected hemisphere compared to the control (Figure 1e), confirming that the damage affected a large portion of the tract.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant increase in axonal diameter proxy.

claim: Other parameters extracted from the MRI analysis are not significantly different between hemispheres in the rat model.
source: The other parameters extracted from the MRI analysis are not significantly different between hemispheres, although there is a tendency of reduced slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time in the injected hemisphere (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a tendency of reduced slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time in the injected hemisphere.
source: The other parameters extracted from the MRI analysis are not significantly different between hemispheres, although there is a tendency of reduced slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time in the injected hemisphere (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: There is a significant effect of the injection on MRI axonal diameter proxy (F1,9=20.3, p=0.001).
source: Through tract-based analysis, we revealed a significant effect of the injection (F1,9=20.3, p=0.001), of the position along the tract (F48,432=83.9, p<0.001) and of their interaction (F48,432=5.7, p=0.003); post-hoc comparisons between injection type, performed for each position and corrected for multiple comparisons, revealed significant differences in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy between ibotenic acid- and saline-injected tracts in most parts of the tract.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: There is a significant effect of position along the tract on MRI axonal diameter proxy (F48,432=83.9, p<0.001).
source: Through tract-based analysis, we revealed a significant effect of the injection (F1,9=20.3, p=0.001), of the position along the tract (F48,432=83.9, p<0.001) and of their interaction (F48,432=5.7, p=0.003); post-hoc comparisons between injection type, performed for each position and corrected for multiple comparisons, revealed significant differences in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy between ibotenic acid- and saline-injected tracts in most parts of the tract.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: There is a significant interaction between injection and position along the tract on MRI axonal diameter proxy (F48,432=5.7, p=0.003).
source: Through tract-based analysis, we revealed a significant effect of the injection (F1,9=20.3, p=0.001), of the position along the tract (F48,432=83.9, p<0.001) and of their interaction (F48,432=5.7, p=0.003); post-hoc comparisons between injection type, performed for each position and corrected for multiple comparisons, revealed significant differences in the mean MRI axonal diameter proxy between ibotenic acid- and saline-injected tracts in most parts of the tract.
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: Significant differences in mean MRI axonal diameter proxy between ibotenic acid- and saline-injected tracts were mostly localized posterior to the injection site.
source: Significant differences were mostly localized posterior to the injection site (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Similar results were obtained in animals undergoing a protocol with lower b-values and a diffusion model not including the Δ dependency (AxCaliber).
source: In the subset of animals undergoing a protocol with lower b-values and a diffusion model not including the Δ dependency (AxCaliber), we obtained similar results (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: There is neuronal loss in the hippocampus in ibotenic acid-injected hemispheres compared to saline-injected hemispheres (p=0.026).
source: When comparing immunofluorescence staining in ibotenic acid- versus saline-injected hemispheres, we confirmed both neuronal loss in the hippocampus (p=0.026, Figure 2a–b) and axonal damage in the fimbria (p=0.047, Figure 2c–d), corresponding to a lower staining intensity of neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) and higher intensity of neurofilament staining in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2a-b.

claim: There is axonal damage in the fimbria in ibotenic acid-injected hemispheres compared to saline-injected hemispheres (p=0.047).
source: When comparing immunofluorescence staining in ibotenic acid- versus saline-injected hemispheres, we confirmed both neuronal loss in the hippocampus (p=0.026, Figure 2a–b) and axonal damage in the fimbria (p=0.047, Figure 2c–d), corresponding to a lower staining intensity of neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) and higher intensity of neurofilament staining in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining shown in Figure 2c-d.

claim: Lower staining intensity of neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) corresponds to neuronal loss in the hippocampus.
source: When comparing immunofluorescence staining in ibotenic acid- versus saline-injected hemispheres, we confirmed both neuronal loss in the hippocampus (p=0.026, Figure 2a–b) and axonal damage in the fimbria (p=0.047, Figure 2c–d), corresponding to a lower staining intensity of neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) and higher intensity of neurofilament staining in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining.

claim: Higher intensity of neurofilament staining corresponds to axonal damage in the fimbria.
source: When comparing immunofluorescence staining in ibotenic acid- versus saline-injected hemispheres, we confirmed both neuronal loss in the hippocampus (p=0.026, Figure 2a–b) and axonal damage in the fimbria (p=0.047, Figure 2c–d), corresponding to a lower staining intensity of neuronal nuclear protein (NeuN) and higher intensity of neurofilament staining in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunofluorescence staining.

claim: No differences were found in the fimbria myelin content using Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) staining.
source: No differences were found in the fimbria myelin content using Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that at the studied time point, axonal structure was significantly altered, but the total myelin content was still preserved.
evidence: This is demonstrated by MBP staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: At the studied time point, axonal structure was significantly altered, but the total myelin content was still preserved.
source: No differences were found in the fimbria myelin content using Myelin Basic Protein (MBP) staining (Figure 2—figure supplement 1), suggesting that at the studied time point, axonal structure was significantly altered, but the total myelin content was still preserved.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of altered neurofilament staining and unchanged MBP staining.

claim: Neurofilament fluorescence intensity is significantly correlated with the axonal diameter proxy measured with MRI (r=0.54, p=0.029).
source: Neurofilament fluorescence intensity was significantly correlated with the axonal diameter proxy measured with MRI (r=0.54, p=0.029) in both the fimbria tract of injected and control hemispheres (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is demonstrated by correlation analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) revealed increased axonal diameter in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid.
source: Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) revealed increased axonal diameter in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid, with no significant reduction in axonal count, indicating limited axonal loss, as reported in Figure 3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by STEM measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: There is no significant reduction in axonal count in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid, indicating limited axonal loss.
source: Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) revealed increased axonal diameter in the hemisphere injected with ibotenic acid, with no significant reduction in axonal count, indicating limited axonal loss, as reported in Figure 3.
evidence: This is demonstrated by STEM measurements shown in Figure 3.

claim: The total brain shrinkage from in vivo to after perfusion was quantified as 28% in three animals.
source: In Figure 3—figure supplement 1, the total brain shrinkage from in vivo to after perfusion was quantified in three animals as 28%.
evidence: This is measured and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Post-fixation with 1% osmium tetroxide gives at least a 15% additional shrinkage.
source: Since the post-fixation with 1% osmium tetroxide gives at least a 15% additional shrinkage (Kinney et al., 2013), the total shrinkage caused by the STEM preparation can be quantified as 39%.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The total shrinkage caused by the STEM preparation can be quantified as 39%.
source: Since the post-fixation with 1% osmium tetroxide gives at least a 15% additional shrinkage (Kinney et al., 2013), the total shrinkage caused by the STEM preparation can be quantified as 39%.
evidence: This is calculated from the measured shrinkage values.

claim: Higher MRI axonal diameter proxy values were found in the NAWM of MS patients compared to controls (p<0.05, corrected).
source: When comparing the MRI axonal diameter proxy in the NAWM of MS patients and controls, we found higher values in the MS group (p<0.05, corrected; Figure 4).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: The differences in MRI axonal diameter proxy were mostly symmetrical across hemispheres in MS patients.
source: The differences were mostly symmetrical across hemispheres and involved all major WM tracts, notably: the corpus callosum, the corticospinal tract, the internal capsule, the corona radiata, the thalamic radiation, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the cingulum, the fornix, the superior longitudinal fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the uncinate fasciculus, and the tapetum.
evidence: This is observed in the spatial distribution of differences.

claim: Increased MRI axonal diameter proxy in MS patients involved all major white matter tracts.
source: The differences were mostly symmetrical across hemispheres and involved all major WM tracts, notably: the corpus callosum, the corticospinal tract, the internal capsule, the corona radiata, the thalamic radiation, the inferior longitudinal fasciculus, the cingulum, the fornix, the superior longitudinal fasciculus, the inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus, the uncinate fasciculus, and the tapetum.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the spatial extent of significant differences.

claim: There is a trend of negative correlation between the magnitude of the MRI axonal diameter proxy in patients and the disease duration.
source: Tract-based spatial statistics unveiled a trend of negative correlation between the magnitude of the MRI axonal diameter proxy in patients and the disease duration, as shown in Figure 5a.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5a.

claim: There is a significant group effect in the ANOVA comparing average values of MRI axonal diameter proxy in the whole white matter between controls, short and long disease duration MS patients (F2,18=9.2, p=0.002).
source: When comparing average values of MRI axonal diameter proxy in the whole white matter (excluding lesions in MS) between groups (controls, short and long disease duration), we report a significant group effect in the ANOVA (F2,18=9.2, p=0.002).
evidence: This is demonstrated by ANOVA statistical analysis.

claim: MS patients with disease onset less than 5 years prior to MRI scan had increased axonal diameter compared to controls (p=0.001, corrected for multiple comparisons).
source: MS patients for whom the disease onset was less than 5 years prior to the MRI scan had increased axonal diameter compared to controls (p=0.001, corrected for multiple comparisons), while this increase was not significant in MS patients with a longer disease course (p=0.18).
evidence: This is demonstrated by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: The increase in axonal diameter was not significant in MS patients with a longer disease course (p=0.18).
source: MS patients for whom the disease onset was less than 5 years prior to the MRI scan had increased axonal diameter compared to controls (p=0.001, corrected for multiple comparisons), while this increase was not significant in MS patients with a longer disease course (p=0.18).
evidence: This is demonstrated by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: No significant associations were found between axonal diameter and EDSS or SDMT.
source: We did not find significant associations between axonal diameter and other tested clinical variables of neurological disability and information processing speed (Expanded Disability Status Scale [EDDS] and Symbol Digit Modalities Test [SDMT]).
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis.

claim: Both the slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time and the restricted signal fraction are significantly reduced in a portion of the normal-appearing white matter in MS.
source: Finally, we tested both group differences and associations with disease duration for the rest of the parameters extracted in the MRI analysis. While both the slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time and the restricted signal fraction are significantly reduced in a portion of the normal-appearing white matter in MS (reported in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), no MRI parameter except the MRI axonal diameter proxy is significantly associated with disease duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: No MRI parameter except the MRI axonal diameter proxy is significantly associated with disease duration.
source: Finally, we tested both group differences and associations with disease duration for the rest of the parameters extracted in the MRI analysis. While both the slope of the extra-axonal radial diffusivity decay for increasing diffusion time and the restricted signal fraction are significantly reduced in a portion of the normal-appearing white matter in MS (reported in Figure 4—figure supplement 1), no MRI parameter except the MRI axonal diameter proxy is significantly associated with disease duration.
evidence: This is demonstrated by statistical analysis.

claim: Early axonal damage in MS manifests through the formation of varicosities and spheroids that enlarge the axonal diameter.
source: Neuropathologically, early axonal damage in MS manifests through the formation of varicosities and spheroids that enlarge the axonal diameter and are associated with impaired axonal transport (Criste et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Varicosities and spheroids in MS are associated with impaired axonal transport.
source: Neuropathologically, early axonal damage in MS manifests through the formation of varicosities and spheroids that enlarge the axonal diameter and are associated with impaired axonal transport (Criste et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Histological postmortem studies report an increase in the mean axonal diameter in MS compared to controls in demyelinating and non-demyelinating areas.
source: Accordingly, histological postmortem (Bergers et al., 2002) and animal studies (Nikić et al., 2011) report an increase in the mean axonal diameter in MS compared to controls in demyelinating and non-demyelinating areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Animal studies report an increase in the mean axonal diameter in MS compared to controls in demyelinating and non-demyelinating areas.
source: Accordingly, histological postmortem (Bergers et al., 2002) and animal studies (Nikić et al., 2011) report an increase in the mean axonal diameter in MS compared to controls in demyelinating and non-demyelinating areas.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The increase in mean axonal diameter is influenced by the higher vulnerability of smaller axons compared to larger ones.
source: This increase is also influenced by the higher vulnerability of smaller axons compared to larger ones (Tallantyre et al., 2010), which implies that smaller axons are lost earlier.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Smaller axons are lost earlier than larger axons in MS.
source: This increase is also influenced by the higher vulnerability of smaller axons compared to larger ones (Tallantyre et al., 2010), which implies that smaller axons are lost earlier.
evidence: This is inferred from the higher vulnerability of smaller axons.

claim: Histological alterations in axonal morphology have been observed in the NAWM of MS brain specimens in the absence of inflammation.
source: Histological alterations in axonal morphology have also been observed in the NAWM of MS brain specimens in the absence of inflammation (Luchicchi et al., 2021), suggesting that an imbalance of axon-myelin units could represent the primary event in MS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: An imbalance of axon-myelin units could represent the primary event in MS pathogenesis.
source: Histological alterations in axonal morphology have also been observed in the NAWM of MS brain specimens in the absence of inflammation (Luchicchi et al., 2021), suggesting that an imbalance of axon-myelin units could represent the primary event in MS pathogenesis.
evidence: This is suggested based on observations in NAWM without inflammation.

claim: An increase in axonal diameter in MS was reported in previous MRI studies.
source: Based on neuropathological evidence, axonal damage in MS would reasonably manifest as an increase in axonal caliber measured with imaging. An increase in axonal diameter in MS was indeed reported in previous MRI studies (Huang et al., 2016), but the results were not validated.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous MRI studies reporting increased axonal diameter in MS were not validated.
source: Based on neuropathological evidence, axonal damage in MS would reasonably manifest as an increase in axonal caliber measured with imaging. An increase in axonal diameter in MS was indeed reported in previous MRI studies (Huang et al., 2016), but the results were not validated.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.

claim: Comparing imaging results with pathological evidence is fundamental to validate multicompartment models for diffusion signals.
source: In the context of multicompartment models for diffusion signals, comparing imaging results with pathological evidence is fundamental to validate the model, as multicompartment models make numerous assumptions and simplifications (to cite a few: fixed diffusivities [Alexander et al., 2010], no exchange [Lasič et al., 2011], indirect account of the volume occupied by myelin [Assaf et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological principle and supported by citations.

claim: Multicompartment models for diffusion signals make numerous assumptions and simplifications.
source: In the context of multicompartment models for diffusion signals, comparing imaging results with pathological evidence is fundamental to validate the model, as multicompartment models make numerous assumptions and simplifications (to cite a few: fixed diffusivities [Alexander et al., 2010], no exchange [Lasič et al., 2011], indirect account of the volume occupied by myelin [Assaf et al., 2008]).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies reported correlations between the axonal diameter measured with MRI and axonal caliber estimated using electron microscopy in healthy tissue.
source: Previous studies reported correlations between the axonal diameter measured with MRI and axonal caliber estimated using electron microscopy in healthy tissue (Barazany et al., 2009), but with a reduced sample size.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Previous studies correlating MRI and electron microscopy measurements of axonal diameter had a reduced sample size.
source: Previous studies reported correlations between the axonal diameter measured with MRI and axonal caliber estimated using electron microscopy in healthy tissue (Barazany et al., 2009), but with a reduced sample size.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of previous work.

claim: No previous studies have demonstrated that AxCaliber is sensitive to axonal damage.
source: In addition, none thus far have demonstrated that AxCaliber is sensitive to axonal damage.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Quantitative comparison between MRI maps and stained sections is severely hampered by the fixation process and other limitations.
source: Quantitative comparison between MRI maps and stained sections is severely hampered by the fixation process and other limitations (Horowitz et al., 2015; Barakovic et al., 2023); here, we used a well-characterized rodent model in which the axonal compartment is selectively damaged.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The approach of using a well-characterized rodent model with selective axonal damage has been previously used to prove the capability of diffusion MRI to dissect astrocyte and microglia reactivity in gray matter.
source: This approach has been previously used to prove the capability of diffusion MRI to dissect astrocyte and microglia reactivity in gray matter (Garcia-Hernandez et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Increased neurofilament staining intensity in the damaged tract demonstrates altered axonal morphology without alteration in the total amount of myelin.
source: Here, we detected increased neurofilament staining intensity in the damaged tract, demonstrating altered axonal morphology without alteration in the total amount of myelin.
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data.

claim: The increase in MRI axonal diameter proxy reflects true morphological axonal alterations, hallmarks of axonal pathology.
source: Electron microscopy and axonal diameter quantification demonstrate that the increase observed in imaging reflects true morphological axonal alterations, hallmarks of axonal pathology.
evidence: This is demonstrated by electron microscopy data.

claim: The correlation between neurofilament staining intensity and the MRI axonal diameter proxy validates the imaging parameter as a marker of axonal damage.
source: The significant correlation between neurofilament staining intensity and the MRI axonal diameter proxy further validates the imaging parameter as a marker of axonal damage, and is compatible with recent work studying the association of MRI metrics sensitive to axonal pathology and the serum neurofilament light chain biomarker in humans (Rahmanzadeh et al., 2021).
evidence: This is inferred from the significant correlation and supported by citation.

claim: Axonal diameter mapping through MRI can detect axonal pathology in vivo and can be used as a biomarker of axonal damage in MS and possibly other neurological diseases.
source: Overall, our preclinical results show that axonal diameter mapping through MRI can detect axonal pathology in vivo and can thus be used as a biomarker of axonal damage in MS and possibly other neurological diseases.
evidence: This is concluded from the preclinical validation results.

claim: There is an ongoing debate on the discrepancy between MRI axonal diameter proxy and axonal diameter measured in fixated tissue using electron microscopy.
source: These results are extremely important given the ongoing debate on the discrepancy between MRI axonal diameter proxy and axonal diameter measured in fixated tissue using electron microscopy.
evidence: This is stated as context for the importance of the findings.

claim: Both MRI and STEM detect a significant increase in the axonal diameter in the rat model.
source: The fact that both MRI and STEM detect a significant increase in the axonal diameter reconciles such findings, demonstrating that while absolute quantification of axonal caliber might differ (with MRI consistently overestimating axonal diameter due to higher weightings of larger axons, and STEM consistently underestimating axonal diameter due to heavy tissue fixation, as shown by our shrinkage analysis), both are sensitive to the same underlying pathological phenomenon.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the experimental results.

claim: MRI consistently overestimates axonal diameter due to higher weightings of larger axons.
source: The fact that both MRI and STEM detect a significant increase in the axonal diameter reconciles such findings, demonstrating that while absolute quantification of axonal caliber might differ (with MRI consistently overestimating axonal diameter due to higher weightings of larger axons, and STEM consistently underestimating axonal diameter due to heavy tissue fixation, as shown by our shrinkage analysis), both are sensitive to the same underlying pathological phenomenon.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of MRI measurements.

claim: STEM consistently underestimates axonal diameter due to heavy tissue fixation.

Notably, the combination of whole brain mapping and a larger sample size uncovered significant negative associations between MRI axonal diameter proxy and disease duration, suggesting enlarged axonal caliber as an early event in MS pathogenesis, as illustrated in Figure 5c.
